conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Dr. Maya Carter, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician here. I specialize in caring for new mothers and the emotional ups and downs that can show up after a baby arrives.

In front of us we have the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually shortened to the EPDS. It’s a brief, 10-question checklist that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting or a judgment of you as a mom; it simply gives us a snapshot of mood and anxiety symptoms that are surprisingly common in the postpartum year.

Everything we discuss stays confidential within our treatment team unless you tell us you might hurt yourself or someone else, in which case we’d work together on keeping everyone safe. We want this to feel like a safe, supportive space where you can speak freely.

I’ll read each question in everyday language, and you can just tell me which response best fits. When we’re finished I’ll add up the numbers privately, share what the score suggests, and we can talk through next steps. Ready to begin?

Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—would you say always, most of the time, sometimes, or hardly ever?

Um… I guess “sometimes.” I still laugh if my husband cracks a joke or if the dog does something silly, but it feels like it takes more effort than it used to. I don’t find myself naturally smiling or laughing the way I did before the baby came.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes. It's not that I never laugh—like, if my husband makes a joke or the dog does something goofy, I still crack up—but it feels kind of forced or distant. I have to remind myself to enjoy the moment instead of just automatically feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Sometimes... I still get little sparks of excitement—like when my mom said she’d come over so I could take a walk by myself—but most of the time it feels pretty flat. I used to be the person who’d count down the days to brunch with friends or a new show dropping, and now it’s more “yeah, that’ll be nice, I guess,” if that makes sense.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah... sometimes. Like, if the baby’s extra fussy and won’t nap, I’ll catch myself thinking I must be doing something wrong—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not reading his cues right. Or if I burn the toast or forget to switch the laundry, I hear this little voice saying, “You can’t even handle simple stuff—no wonder you’re overwhelmed.” I know it’s not totally fair, but those thoughts still pop up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most of the time. It’s like there’s this low-level buzz in my chest even when everything seems fine. I’ll lie down after finally getting the baby to sleep and suddenly my heart’s racing and I’m running through all the what-ifs—what if he stops breathing, what if I’m not making enough milk, what if I miss some sign that he’s sick. Nothing specific triggered it, but the worry just sits there.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes. I’ll be rocking the baby in the middle of the night and out of nowhere my chest gets tight, like I can’t quite catch a full breath, and my mind jumps to “what if I can’t do this?” It passes after a few minutes, but those waves of panic still catch me off guard.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, most of the time. It feels like the second I finish one feeding, the laundry’s already piled up again, the dishes are staring at me, and I can’t remember whether I’ve eaten. I keep telling myself it’s normal with a newborn, but it still feels like I’m drowning in little tasks I can’t quite keep up with.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Sometimes. I wouldn’t say I’m miserable all day, but when evening comes my mind just keeps spinning—did I sterilize the bottles, is he gaining enough weight, will he wake up right after I fall asleep? Some nights it takes me an hour or two to drift off, even when the baby’s already out.
I have felt sad or miserable

Sometimes. It’s not there every minute, but it hits me in quiet moments—like when I’m nursing at 3 a.m. and the house is dark, I’ll just feel this wave of sadness wash over me. I’ll look at his tiny face and think I should be overflowing with joy, but instead there’s this heavy, empty feeling that lingers for a while before it lifts.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Hardly ever. I’ve teared up a couple of times—like when the baby wouldn’t latch and my nipples felt like they were on fire—but I haven’t actually sat down and cried a full-on bout. Mostly I just feel kind of numb or tired instead of weepy.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
Never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – EPDS-Style Review

**Symptoms / Concerns endorsed**  
- Anhedonia: diminished enjoyment, “flat” mood, forced laughter (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame (Q3)  
- Persistent, non-specific anxiety & episodic panic (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed, “drowning in tasks” (Q6)  
- Sleep-onset difficulty linked to racing worries (Q7)  
- Intermittent sadness / emptiness without pervasive tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  
- No self-harm or suicidal ideation (Q10)

**Pattern**: Predominantly mixed anxiety–mood presentation with functional impact but no safety indicators.

**Screening significance**  
Score estimate (0–30): ≈ 13–15 → above typical cut-off (≥10) for further evaluation for postpartum depression and/or anxiety.

**Risk factors noted**  
- Daily anhedonia and guilt cognitions  
- Frequent anxiety and occasional nocturnal panic episodes  
- Sleep disruption secondary to worry  
- Subjective inability to cope with routine infant care demands

**Observation summary**  
Patient reports multiple mood and anxiety symptoms exceeding normal postpartum adjustment; no self-harm ideation elicited. Recommend formal clinical interview (DSM-5-TR criteria) to clarify diagnosis and determine need for psychosocial or pharmacologic intervention.
